children.text: A deep bay that served as a Spanish and then American naval base for about a century has become a freeport zone, great for families to enjoy primeval jungle experiences, a marine theme park, a safari, World War II wreck diving, and quiet beaches.

Subic Bay is a natural bay cutting deep into Luzon's west coast, between the Zambales mountain range and the Bataan Peninsula. Deep waters and calm seas, sheltered by surrounding mountains, led the 19th-century Spanish navy to build a shipyard here, and from

the United States took it over and grew it into one of the largest overseas naval bases in the Pacific. During the Korean and Vietnam wars, it was a key supply and repair base for the U.S. Pacific Fleet. When the Philippine Senate refused to extend the base agreement in
, U.S. forces left in
November 1992
, and the base was converted into the Subic Bay Freeport Zone (SBMA).

The base era's straight roads, wide lawns, and old naval buildings lining the coast are now used as hotels, restaurants, a yacht club, and duty-free shops. Traffic law enforcement is strict and the streets are clean inside the freeport zone, giving it a noticeably different atmosphere from other Philippine cities. Right next door is Olongapo City, which thrived during the base era and offers a contrasting scene with its down-to-earth markets and eateries.

Subic's real draw is the nature that spreads out right behind the town. Spared from development because it was a restricted military zone during the base era, the Subic rainforest is one of the finest primary lowland forests on Luzon, home to birds endemic to the Philippines and colonies of the giant golden-crowned flying fox, one of the world's largest bats. The Indigenous Aeta people taught U.S. troops jungle survival skills during the base era, and today they share that knowledge with visitors.

Beneath the water lie shipwrecks sunk during the Spanish-American War and World War II, making this one of the best wreck-diving destinations in Southeast Asia. With jungle experiences, a marine theme park, a safari, beaches, and duty-free shopping all in one place, it's especially well suited to family trips with children and weekend getaways during a stay in Manila or Clark.

The Subic Bay Freeport Zone covers 67,452 ha in total, but the fenced core area is about 14,000 ha, and about 10,000 ha of lowland tropical forest remains within it. The sights fall into three main clusters. Along the Waterfront Road next to Olongapo are hotels, restaurants, the yacht club, shopping malls, and the Spanish Gate, the old gateway from the days of the Spanish naval shipyard; in the forest around the former Cubi Point naval air station are JEST Camp, Treetop Adventure, and the bat colony; and in the Ilanin Forest and on Camayan Point to the southwest are Zoobic Safari, Ocean Adventure, and Camayan Beach. You need a car to get between the clusters, so it works best to cover two clusters a day.
A marine park that opened in
on Camayan Point, a former ammunition pier, where you can watch dolphin, sea lion, and false killer whale shows in sea pens connected directly to the bay. It's open daily from
9 AM–5 PM
, and admission is
for adults (13 and over) and
for children 12 and under, including all shows. Hands-on programs such as swimming with dolphins cost extra and must be booked in advance; check the
official website
for the latest prices.

A zoo set in the Ilanin Forest whose signature attraction is the Tiger Safari, where a safari vehicle takes you through the tiger enclosure, followed by a crocodile farm (Croco Loco), a snake exhibit, and animal shows. It's open daily from
8 AM–4 PM
, but last admission is at
2 PM
. Regular admission is about
for adults and about
for children (about
120 cm
tall or under), plus a separate
environmental and tourism fee paid on site; allow
2.5–4 hours
to see it all.
JEST Camp, in the Mau forest above Cubi Point, was used by the U.S. military as a jungle survival training ground in the
; today Aeta instructors demonstrate how to cook rice in bamboo, start a fire, and find edible plants. Options range from a forest walk of
1–2 hours
to a
6-hour

program with lunch, so confirm the schedule in advance by phone or email. The Pamulaklakin forest trail on Binictican Drive is run by the Aeta community itself, and you can walk the forest with an Indigenous guide, relax by the river, or even camp.

An adventure park in the same Cubi Point forest as JEST Camp, with the Canopy Ride, where you hang from a cable and glide over the forest; the Superman Ride, where you fly lying face down; the Tree Drop, a fall from about
high; and the Canopy Walk, which links the trees. Packages that bundle the activities cost about
per person, and the courses are divided so that everyone from children to adults can enjoy them.
The armored cruiser USS New York, scuttled in
to keep it out of Japanese hands, is a massive
wreck lying at a depth of about
. There are also many wrecks that even beginners can dive, such as the El Capitan at about
and the San Quintin (about
), which Spain sank in
to block the mouth of the bay. A fun dive costs about
per dive, and the water is clearest in
February–May

SBMA Beach and the boardwalk along the Waterfront Road are popular spots for a sunset stroll. Grande Island at the mouth of the bay still has the remains of Fort Wint, a U.S. coastal fort completed in
, and it's about
20–30 minutes

by boat from the pier on the Waterfront Road. The island operator sells day packages that bundle the boat, lunch, and a guided tour, but schedules change often, so check ahead. Camayan Beach, run by the same company as Ocean Adventure, is reachable by car and offers snorkeling and kayaking.
The forests around Cubi Point and Triboa are home to a large colony where the giant golden-crowned flying fox, one of the world's largest bats with a wingspan of up to
, lives alongside the Philippine giant fruit bat. A

survey counted about 26,000 bats, but reports say human disturbance has reduced the number to around 10,000. By day you can see them sleeping upside down from the branches, and at dusk the spectacle of them taking off all at once in search of food, so observe quietly.

blocks.title: Duty-free shopping and a walk along the yacht harbor

children.text: Duty-free supermarkets such as Royal Duty Free, in business for over 30 years, and Puregold Duty Free sell imported groceries, liquor, and household goods. Browse Harbor Point Mall on Rizal Highway, then spend a leisurely evening strolling the waterfront around the Subic Bay Yacht Club, where yachts crowd the marina.

After multiple dives in a day, you need to wait at least
18 hours
before flying, so skip diving the day before you fly out of Clark or Manila.
From Manila, take NLEX north, switch to SCTEX, and at the Tipo exit continue onto the Subic Freeport Expressway (SFEX,
8.8 km
); you'll pass the SBMA checkpoint and enter the freeport zone. The trip is about
and takes
2.5–3 hours
, with tolls of about
one way for a car (NLEX about

). From Clark, it's about
1 hour
via SCTEX. Inside the freeport zone, speed limits, seatbelt use, and the ban on using a phone while driving are strictly enforced.
Buses to Olongapo leave from the Victory Liner terminals in Cubao, Pasay, PITX (Parañaque), and Caloocan. From Cubao, buses depart frequently from early morning until night and take about
3–3.5 hours
. Fares were about
for regular air-conditioned buses and about
for express buses, but provincial bus fares per kilometer went up on
September 28, 2026

, so check the actual fare when you buy your ticket. From the Olongapo terminal, the freeport zone's main gate is a short jeepney or tricycle ride away, and once inside the gate you take the zone's own taxis.
From the bus stop on the arrivals level of Clark International Airport (CRK) Terminal 2, Victory Liner buses run to Olongapo via Dau around 10 times a day, taking about
1 hour 30 minutes
for a fare of about
. From Angeles or central Clark, an Olongapo-bound bus from the Dau terminal takes about
1.5–2 hours
. By rental car or hired vehicle from the airport, it takes about
1 hour
If you're flying in directly from overseas, such as from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest, and Subic is about
1 hour
from the airport by car. From Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), it's
3–4 hours

by car, or you can take a Victory Liner bus from the Pasay or PITX terminal. Subic Bay International Airport (SFS), converted from the former Cubi Point naval air station, currently has no scheduled passenger flights.

Jeepneys and tricycles can't enter the freeport zone; instead, SUV taxis bearing official zone markings and vehicle numbers operate there. They have no meters and charge by distance, so agree on the fare before you get in. Since the sights are far apart, a rental car (about
a day for a compact) or a hired car with a driver is the most convenient option, and the beaches and waterfront are great to explore by bike.
The Zambales coast, where Subic lies, is one of the regions of the Philippines with the most distinct dry and rainy seasons. In the
November–April
dry season it hardly rains and the sea is calm, making it good for beaches, island trips, and diving alike.
December–February
in particular is cool and clear, pleasant for visiting the outdoor theme parks.
March–April
is hot, with daytime highs of about
, but the water is warm and visibility is good, making it the peak diving season.
In the rainy season from
mid-May to October
, the southwest monsoon (habagat) blows straight onto the west coast, and most of the roughly 3,400 mm of annual rainfall pours down during this period. In
July–September

, more than 700 mm falls each month, with heavy rain lasting for days at a time, and when a typhoon hits, boat services and diving are completely suspended. Theme parks and shopping are still possible, but it's best not to schedule beach days.
During long weekends, Holy Week, and the summer school break (
April–May
), hotels fill up with families from Manila and Clark. Visiting on a weekday means much shorter waits at the theme parks. In
December
, Olongapo City's Ulo ng Apo Festival runs all month long, with parades and performances.

Accommodation is clustered along the Waterfront Road inside the freeport zone. There are hotels converted from old naval officers' quarters, resorts overlooking the bay, and family-friendly condo hotels, at about
a night. Forest resorts or boutique hotels near the yacht harbor are good for a quiet stay. To save money, you can stay at budget to midrange lodgings (about
a night) in Olongapo town or at nearby Barrio Barretto Beach.

Thanks to its base-era legacy, Subic has plenty of American-style steak, burger, and barbecue restaurants, and the area around the yacht harbor is lined with restaurants where you can eat seafood while looking out at the sea. In Olongapo town, you can enjoy Filipino-style seafood and casual local eateries at low prices. The duty-free shops sell imported American and Australian groceries and wine at relatively low prices, so Korean residents of the Philippines sometimes come here to shop. The area has deep ties to Korea — since
, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries has been building ships again at the former Hanjin Heavy Industries shipyard, which closed in
— so there are also a few Korean restaurants and Korean grocery stores.

Long-time favorites include Texas Joe's House of Ribs, an American barbecue joint serving smoked ribs and brisket, and Xtremely Xpresso Cafe, known for its strong coffee and big pizzas. The best-known upscale seaside stay is The Lighthouse Marina Resort, whose lighthouse-shaped building is its signature, at around
a night.
For Zoobic Safari and Ocean Adventure, buying online in advance or choosing a bundle deal is often cheaper than paying at the gate.
Enter the theme parks early in the morning. In the afternoon, tour groups crowd in and the midday heat makes the animals sluggish too.
Driving rules are strict inside the freeport zone. Speeding, not wearing a seatbelt, and using a phone while driving are all immediately enforced.
For the jungle trails, bring long pants, sneakers, and insect repellent. Long socks are good during the wet season, when leeches appear.
If you're planning to dive, use a local shop experienced with wrecks. For the deep USS New York, Advanced certification or higher is recommended.
Duty-free stores carry plenty of imported goods, but some items cost more than at big supermarkets in town, so compare prices on things you buy often.
The waterfront coastal road at sunset is the highlight of a trip to Subic. Take a walk or bike ride around
5 PM
The checkpoint between Olongapo town and the freeport zone gets congested at rush hour, so allow extra travel time.
Notices on events in the freeport zone, road closures, and operations during typhoons are posted on the
official website
of the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA). Check it once before long weekends or big events.
During heavy wet-season rain, jungle trails and valleys carry a risk of flash floods and landslides. If management restricts access, don't push your way in.
Always follow the staff's instructions for animal encounters at Zoobic Safari. Don't put your hands or food out the window.
Subic Bay has strong currents and heavy vessel traffic. Avoid swimming outside designated beach areas.
Fruit bats are a protected species. Don't disturb their habitat with noise or light, and avoid drone photography as well.
In Olongapo town, watch out for pickpockets and inflated prices, and don't walk around alone late at night.
In
August 2026
, nearly a month of heavy southwest monsoon rain flooded some roads inside the freeport zone and the approach road to the Kalayaan Gate, and Olongapo City declared a state of calamity on
September 1
. During the rainy season, check PAGASA weather warnings and SBMA notices, and allow plenty of travel time.
The Oryoku Maru, off the mouth of the Kalaklan River, is a war grave where hundreds of Allied prisoners of war died in a U.S. air raid in
December 1944
, so diving there is prohibited. In
, the U.S. Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) carried out recovery work for remains at the site.
